title: Chapter 26. Of Civil Laws
paragraphs: By CIVIL LAWS I mean the laws that men are bound to observe because they are members not of this or that commonwealth in particular, but of a commonwealth. For the knowledge of particular laws belongs to those who profess the study of the laws of their several countries; but the knowledge of civil law in general belongs to anyone. The ancient law of Rome was called their civil law, from the word civitas, which means a commonwealth. And those countries which, having been under the Roman Empire and governed by that law, still retain such part of it as they think fit, call that part the civil law, to distinguish it from the rest of their own civil laws. But that is not what I intend to speak of here; my design is not to show what is law here and there, but what law is — as Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and various others have done, without taking on themselves the profession of the study of law.

First, then, it is plain that law in general is not counsel but command; nor is it the command of any man to any man, but only of one whose command is addressed to a person already obliged to obey him. As for civil law, it adds only the name of the person commanding — which is Persona Civitatis, the person of the commonwealth.

With that in mind, I define civil law as follows: 'CIVIL LAW is, to every subject, those rules which the commonwealth has commanded him — by word, writing, or some other sufficient sign of its will — to make use of for the distinction of right and wrong; that is, of what is contrary, and what is not contrary, to the rule.'

In this definition, everything is evident at first sight. Every man sees that some laws are addressed to all subjects in general; some to particular provinces; some to particular vocations; and some to particular men; and are therefore laws to every one to whom the command is directed, and to no one else. He sees also that laws are the rules of just and unjust, since an act is reputed unjust only when it is contrary to some law; that none can make laws but the commonwealth, because our subjection is to the commonwealth alone; and that commands must be signified by sufficient signs, because otherwise a man would not know how to obey them. And so whatever can be deduced by necessary consequence from this definition ought to be acknowledged for truth. I draw from it what follows.

1. The legislator in all commonwealths is the sovereign alone — whether one man, as in a monarchy, or one assembly of men, as in a democracy or aristocracy. For the legislator is the one who makes the law. And the commonwealth alone prescribes and commands the observance of the rules we call law; therefore the commonwealth is the legislator. But the commonwealth is no person, and has no capacity to do anything except through its representative (the sovereign); and therefore the sovereign is the sole legislator. For the same reason, none but the sovereign can repeal a law once made; because a law is not repealed except by another law, which forbids it to be put into execution.

2. The sovereign of a commonwealth, whether an assembly or one man, is not subject to the civil laws. Having the power to make and repeal laws, he may when he pleases free himself from that subjection by repealing the laws that trouble him and making new ones; and consequently he was free before. For a man who can free himself whenever he wills was never truly bound. Nor is it possible for any person to be bound to himself: for the one who can bind can release; and so the one bound only to himself is not bound at all.

3. When long use takes on the authority of a law, it is not the length of time that gives the authority, but the will of the sovereign signified by his silence (for silence is sometimes an argument of consent); and it is no longer law than the sovereign shall be silent on it. So if the sovereign has a question of right grounded not on his present will but on laws formerly made, the length of time shall be no detriment to his right, but the question shall be judged by equity — that is, by what is fair, apart from the letter of the law. For many unjust actions, and unjust sentences, go uncontrolled for longer than any man can remember. Our lawyers account no customs to be law except those that are reasonable, and hold that evil customs are to be abolished; but the judgement of what is reasonable, and of what is to be abolished, belongs to the one who makes the law — which is the sovereign assembly, or monarch.

4. The law of nature and the civil law contain each other, and are of equal extent. The laws of nature — consisting in equity, justice, gratitude, and the other moral virtues that depend on these — in the condition of mere nature (as I said before, at the end of chapter 15) are not properly laws but qualities that dispose men to peace and to obedience. Once a commonwealth is settled, then they are actually laws, and not before, being then the commands of the commonwealth, and therefore civil laws as well; for it is the sovereign power that obliges men to obey them. In the disputes of private men, to declare what is equity, what is justice, and what is moral virtue, and to make these declarations binding, requires the ordinances of the sovereign power and the punishments to be ordained for those who break them; and these ordinances are therefore part of the civil law. The law of nature is therefore part of the civil law in all commonwealths of the world. And reciprocally the civil law is part of the dictates of nature. For justice — that is, the keeping of covenants and the giving to every man his own — is a dictate of the law of nature. But every subject in a commonwealth has covenanted to obey the civil law (either with one another, when they assemble to make a common representative, or with the representative himself, one by one, as when, subdued by the sword, they promise obedience to receive their lives); and so obedience to the civil law is also part of the law of nature. Civil and natural law are not different kinds, but different parts of law — one part being written, called civil; the other unwritten, natural. But the right of nature — that is, the natural liberty of man — may by the civil law be cut back and restrained. Indeed, the end of making laws is no other than such restraint, without which there can be no possibility of peace. Law was brought into the world for nothing else than to limit the natural liberty of particular men in such a way that they would not hurt but help one another, and join together against a common enemy.

5. If the sovereign of one commonwealth subdues a people that have lived under other written laws, and afterwards governs them by the same laws under which they were governed before, those laws are still the civil laws of the victor, and not of the vanquished commonwealth. For the legislator is the one not by whose authority the laws were first made, but by whose authority they now continue to be laws. And so where there are various provinces within the dominion of a commonwealth, and various laws in those provinces (commonly called the customs of each province), we are not to understand that such customs have their force only from length of time, but that they were anciently written or otherwise made known as the constitutions and statutes of their sovereigns, and are now laws not by virtue of prescription — that is, a right created merely by long custom — but by the constitutions of their present sovereigns. But if an unwritten law is generally observed throughout all the provinces of a dominion, and no iniquity appears in its use, that law can be nothing but a law of nature, equally binding all mankind.

6. Since then all laws, written and unwritten, get their authority and their force from the will of the commonwealth — that is, from the will of the representative, which in a monarchy is the monarch and in other commonwealths the sovereign assembly — a man may wonder how it comes that such opinions are found in the books of eminent lawyers in various commonwealths, opinions which directly or by consequence make the legislative power depend on private men or subordinate judges. For example: 'The Common Law has no controller but the Parliament' — which is true only where a parliament has the sovereign power, and cannot be assembled or dissolved except at its own discretion. For if there is a right in anyone else to dissolve them, there is also a right to control them, and consequently to control their controlling. And if there is no such right, then the controller of laws is not Parlamentum (Parliament alone) but Rex In Parlamento (the king in Parliament). And where a parliament is sovereign, if it should assemble ever so many, or ever so wise, men from the countries subject to them, for whatever cause, no one will believe that such an assembly has thereby acquired a legislative power. Likewise: 'The two arms of a commonwealth are force and justice; the first of which is in the king, the other deposited in the hands of the Parliament' — as if a commonwealth could subsist in which the force lay in any hand which justice had not the authority to command and to govern.

7. That law can never be against reason, our lawyers agree; and that it is not the letter (that is, every construction of it) but what is according to the intention of the legislator that is the law. And that is true. But the question is, whose reason is it that shall be received for law? It is not meant of any private reason — for then there would be as much contradiction in the laws as there is in the Schools. Nor yet (as Sir Edward Coke makes it, upon Littleton, lib.2, ch.6, fol.97.b) is it 'an artificial perfection of reason, gotten by long study, observation, and experience' (as his was). For it is possible that long study may increase and confirm erroneous judgments; and where men build on false grounds, the more they build, the greater is the ruin. And among those who study and observe with equal time and diligence, the reasons and resolutions reached are, and must remain, discordant. So it is not the juris prudentia, the wisdom, of subordinate judges, but the reason of this our artificial man the commonwealth, and his command, that makes law. And the commonwealth, being in its representative only one person, cannot easily produce contradiction in the laws; and when it does, the same reason can take it away by interpretation or by alteration. In all courts of justice, the sovereign (who is the person of the commonwealth) is the one who judges; the subordinate judge ought to have regard to the reason that moved his sovereign to make such a law, so that his sentence may be in keeping with it. Then it is his sovereign's sentence; otherwise it is his own — and an unjust one.

8. From this — that the law is a command, and that a command consists in the declaration or making known of the will of the one who commands, by voice, writing, or some other sufficient evidence of the same — we may understand that the command of the commonwealth is law only to those who have the means to take notice of it. Over natural fools (that is, those born without the capacity to reason), children, or madmen there is no law, any more than there is over brute beasts; nor are they capable of the title of just or unjust, because they never had the power to make a covenant, or to understand its consequences; and consequently never undertook to authorise the actions of any sovereign, as those who make themselves into a commonwealth must do. And as with those from whom nature, or accident, has taken away the notice of all laws in general, so also every man from whom any accident (not arising from his own default) has taken away the means of taking notice of any particular law is excused if he does not observe it; and to speak properly, that law is no law to him. It is therefore necessary to consider here what arguments and signs are sufficient for the knowledge of what the law is — that is, of what the sovereign's will is — in monarchies as in other forms of government.

First, if a law obliges all the subjects without exception, and is not written, nor otherwise published in places where they may take notice of it, it is a law of nature. For whatever men are to take knowledge of as law, not on others' words but every one from his own reason, must be such as is agreeable to the reason of all men; and no law can be that except the law of nature. The laws of nature therefore need no publishing or proclamation, being contained in this single sentence, approved by all the world: 'Do not that to another which you would think it unreasonable to be done by another to yourself.'

Second, if a law obliges only some class or rank of men, or one particular man, and is not written or published by word, then again it is a law of nature, known by the same arguments and signs that distinguish those in that condition from other subjects. For whatever law is not written, or in some way published by the one who makes it law, can be known only by the reason of the one who is to obey it; and it is therefore also a law not only civil but natural. For example, if the sovereign employs a public minister without written instructions on what to do, the minister is obliged to take the dictates of reason for his instructions. If the sovereign makes him a judge, the judge is to take notice that his sentence ought to be according to the reason of his sovereign — which, being always understood to be equity, he is bound to by the law of nature. Or if an ambassador, he is (in all things not covered by his written instructions) to take as his instruction what reason dictates to be most conducive to his sovereign's interest; and so of all other ministers of the sovereignty, public or private. All these instructions of natural reason may be summed up under the one name of fidelity, which is a branch of natural justice.

The law of nature excepted, it belongs to the essence of all other laws to be made known to every man who shall be obliged to obey them — either by word, by writing, or by some other act known to proceed from the sovereign authority. For the will of another cannot be understood except by his own word or act, or by inference taken from his scope and purpose; which in the person of the commonwealth is to be supposed always consistent with equity and reason. In ancient times, before letters were in common use, the laws were often put into verse, so that the unlettered people, taking pleasure in singing or reciting them, might the more easily keep them in memory. For the same reason Solomon advises a man to bind the Ten Commandments (Prov. 7:3) upon his ten fingers. And of the law that Moses gave the people of Israel at the renewing of the covenant (Deut. 11:19), he bids them teach it to their children, by discoursing of it both at home and on the way, going to bed and rising up, and to write it on the posts and doors of their houses; and (Deut. 31:12) to assemble the people — man, woman, and child — to hear it read.

Nor is it enough that the law be written and published; there must also be plain signs that it proceeds from the will of the sovereign. For private men, when they have, or think they have, force enough to secure their unjust designs and bring them safely to their ambitious ends, may publish for laws whatever they please, without — or against — the legislative authority. So what is required is not only a declaration of the law, but also sufficient signs of its author and of his authority. The author, or legislator, is supposed in every commonwealth to be evident, because he is the sovereign — who, having been constituted by the consent of every one, is supposed by every one to be sufficiently known. And though the ignorance and complacency of men is for the most part such that, when the memory of the first constitution of their commonwealth has worn out, they do not consider by whose power they are protected from their enemies, by whose power their industry is shielded, and by whose power they are righted when injury is done them, yet because no one who reflects can question it, no excuse can be drawn from ignorance of where the sovereignty is placed. It is a dictate of natural reason, and consequently an evident law of nature, that no man ought to weaken the power whose protection he has himself demanded, or knowingly accepted against others. So who the sovereign is, no man, except by his own fault (whatever evil men suggest), can make any doubt about. The difficulty lies in the evidence of the authority derived from him; and the removal of that difficulty depends on knowledge of the public registers, public counsels, public ministers, and public seals — by which all laws are sufficiently verified.
'Verified,' I say, not 'authorised'; for verification is only the testimony and the record, not the authority of the law, which consists in the command of the sovereign alone.

If, then, a man has a question of injury depending on the law of nature — that is, on common equity — the sentence of the judge who, by commission, has authority to hear such cases is a sufficient verification of the law of nature in that individual case. For though the advice of one who professes the study of the law is useful for avoiding contention, it is only advice; the judge must tell men what the law is, upon the hearing of the controversy.

But when the question is one of injury, or of crime, upon a written law, every man, by going to the registers (himself or through others), may, if he wishes, be sufficiently informed before he does the injury or commits the crime whether it is an injury or not. Indeed he ought to do so: for when a man doubts whether the act he is about to do is just or unjust, and may inform himself if he chooses, then to do it is unlawful. In the same way, the man who supposes himself injured in a case determined by the written law, which he himself or others may see and consider, acts unjustly if he complains before consulting the law, and betrays a disposition rather to vex other men than to demand his own right.

If the question is one of obedience to a public officer, to have seen his commission, with the public seal, and to have heard it read — or to have had the means to be informed of it, if a man wanted — is a sufficient verification of his authority. For every man is obliged to do his best endeavour to inform himself of all written laws that may concern his own future actions.

Once the legislator is known, and the laws — either by writing or by the light of nature — are sufficiently published, there is still another very important condition lacking before they are binding. For it is not the letter, but the intent, or meaning — that is, the authentic interpretation of the law (which is the sense of the legislator) — that is the nature of the law. And so the interpretation of all laws depends on the sovereign authority; and the interpreters can be none but those whom the sovereign (to whom alone the subject owes obedience) shall appoint. For otherwise, by the craft of an interpreter, the law may be made to bear a sense contrary to that of the sovereign — by which means the interpreter becomes the legislator.

All laws, written and unwritten, need interpretation. The unwritten law of nature is easy to those who without partiality or passion make use of their natural reason, and therefore leaves its violators without excuse. But almost everyone is blinded by self-love or some other passion in at least some cases, and so the law of nature has nevertheless become the most obscure of all laws, and consequently the one with the greatest need of able interpreters. The written laws, if short, are easily misinterpreted from the various meanings of a word or two; if long, they are more obscure still from the various meanings of many words. So that no written law, delivered in few or in many words, can be well understood without a perfect understanding of the final causes — that is, the purposes — for which the law was made; knowledge of those purposes lies with the legislator. To him therefore there can be no knot in the law that is insoluble — either by finding out the ends that may untie it, or by making whatever ends he wills (as Alexander did with his sword, cutting the Gordian knot), by his legislative power; which no other interpreter can do.
The authentic interpretation of the law is not the interpretation of writers.

The interpretation of the laws of nature, in a commonwealth, does not depend on the books of moral philosophy. The authority of writers, without the authority of the commonwealth, does not make their opinions law, however true they may be. What I have written in this treatise about the moral virtues, and their necessity for the procuring and maintaining of peace, though it is evident truth, is not therefore at once law; it is law because in all commonwealths of the world it is part of the civil law. For though it is naturally reasonable, it is by the sovereign power that it is law. Otherwise it would be a great error to call the laws of nature unwritten laws, of which we see so many volumes published — and in them so many contradictions, both of one another and of themselves.
The interpreter of the law is the judge, giving sentence viva voce — that is, by word of mouth — in every particular case.

The interpretation of the law of nature is the sentence of the judge constituted by the sovereign authority to hear and decide such controversies as depend on it; and it consists in the application of the law to the present case. For in the act of judicature, the judge does no more than consider whether the demand of the party is consistent with natural reason and equity; and the sentence he gives is therefore the interpretation of the law of nature; which interpretation is authentic, not because it is his private sentence, but because he gives it by the authority of the sovereign — by which it becomes the sovereign's sentence, which is law for that time, to the parties pleading.
The sentence of a judge does not bind him, nor any other judge, to give the like sentence in like cases ever afterward.

But because every judge, subordinate or sovereign, is capable of erring in a judgement of equity, if afterward, in another like case, he finds it more consistent with equity to give a contrary sentence, he is obliged to do it. No man's error becomes his own law, nor obliges him to persist in it. Nor (for the same reason) does it become a law to other judges, even if they have sworn to follow it. For though a wrong sentence given by authority of the sovereign — if he knows and allows it, in laws that are mutable — be a constitution of a new law, in cases in which every little circumstance is the same; yet in immutable laws, such as are the laws of nature, such sentences are no laws to the same or to other judges in like cases ever after. Princes succeed one another; one judge passes, another comes; nay, heaven and earth shall pass, but not one tittle — that is, not the smallest stroke — of the law of nature shall pass, for it is the eternal law of God. So all the sentences of preceding judges that have ever been cannot together make a law contrary to natural equity; nor can any examples of former judges warrant an unreasonable sentence, or discharge the present judge from the trouble of studying what is equity (in the case he is to judge) from the principles of his own natural reason. For example, it is against the law of nature to punish the innocent; and innocent is the man who acquits himself judicially, and is acknowledged for innocent by the judge. Put the case now that a man is accused of a capital crime, and, seeing the power and malice of some enemy, and the frequent corruption and partiality of judges, runs away for fear of the outcome — and is afterwards taken, brought to a legal trial, makes it sufficiently appear that he was not guilty of the crime, and being acquitted of it, is nevertheless condemned to lose his goods. This is a plain condemnation of the innocent. I say therefore that there is no place in the world where this can be an interpretation of a law of nature, or be made law by the sentences of preceding judges who had done the same. For the one who judged it first judged unjustly; and no injustice can be a pattern of judgement for succeeding judges. A written law may forbid innocent men to flee, and they may be punished for fleeing. But that fleeing from fear of injury should be taken as presumption of guilt, after a man has already been judicially absolved of the crime, is contrary to the nature of a presumption — which has no place after judgement has been given. Yet this is set down by a great lawyer for the common law of England: 'If a man,' he says, 'who is innocent is accused of a felony, and flees for fear of it — although he is judicially acquitted of the felony, yet if it is found that he fled because of the felony, he shall, despite his innocence, forfeit all his goods, chattels (that is, his personal property), debts, and dues. For as to their forfeiture, the law will admit no proof against the presumption in law grounded on his flight.' Here you see an innocent man, judicially acquitted, despite his innocence (when no written law forbade him to flee), condemned after his acquittal, on a mere presumption in law, to lose all the goods he has. If the law grounds on his flight a presumption of the fact (which was capital), the sentence ought to have been capital; if the presumption were not of the fact, then for what should he lose his goods? This therefore is no law of England; nor is the condemnation grounded on a presumption of law, but on the presumption of the judges. It is also against law to say that no proof shall be admitted against a presumption of law. For all judges, sovereign and subordinate, if they refuse to hear proof, refuse to do justice; and though the sentence be just, the judges who condemn without hearing the proofs offered are unjust judges, and their presumption is mere prejudice, which no man ought to bring with him to the seat of justice, whatever precedent judgements or examples he may pretend to follow. There are other matters of this nature in which men's judgements have been perverted by trusting to precedents; but this is enough to show that, though the sentence of a judge is law to the party pleading, it is no law to any judge who succeeds him in office.

In the same way, when the question is the meaning of written laws, the one who writes a commentary on them is not their interpreter. For commentaries are commonly more open to frivolous objection than the text, and so need other commentaries; and so there is no end of such interpretation. Therefore, unless there is an interpreter authorised by the sovereign, from whom the subordinate judges are not to depart, the interpreter can only be the ordinary judges, in the same way as they are in cases of the unwritten law; and their sentences are to be taken by the litigants as laws in that particular case, but not as binding other judges, in like cases, to give like judgements. For a judge may err in the interpretation even of written laws; but no error of a subordinate judge can change the law, which is the general sentence of the sovereign.

In written laws, men commonly distinguish between the letter and the meaning of the law. When by 'the letter' is meant whatever can be gathered from the bare words, the distinction is well taken. For the meanings of almost all words are either in themselves, or in their metaphorical use, ambiguous, and may be argued into many senses; but there is only one sense of the law. But if by 'the letter' is meant the literal sense, then the letter and the meaning, or intent, of the law are one and the same. For the literal sense is what the legislator is always supposed to intend by equity; and it would be a great affront for a judge to think otherwise of the sovereign. He ought therefore, if the words of the law do not fully authorise a reasonable sentence, to supply it with the law of nature; or if the case is difficult, to defer judgement until he has received more ample authority. For example: a written law ordains that the man thrust out of his house by force shall be restored by force. It happens that a man through negligence leaves his house empty, and on returning is kept out by force — for which case no special law has been made. It is plain that this case is contained in the same law; for otherwise there is no remedy for him at all, which must be supposed to be against the intention of the legislator. Again, the word of the law commands judging according to the evidence; a man is falsely accused of a fact which the judge saw himself done by another and not by the accused. In this case neither shall the letter of the law be followed to the condemnation of the innocent, nor shall the judge give sentence against the evidence of the witnesses — because the letter of the law is to the contrary; but he shall procure from the sovereign that another be made judge, and himself become witness. So the inconvenience that follows from the bare words of a written law may lead a judge to the intention of the law, and so to interpret it better — though no inconvenience can warrant a sentence against the law. For every judge of right and wrong is not a judge of what is convenient or inconvenient for the commonwealth.

The abilities required in a good interpreter of the law — that is, in a good judge — are not the same as an advocate's, namely deep study of the laws. For a judge, as he ought to take notice of the fact from none but the witnesses, ought also to take notice of the law from nothing but the statutes and constitutions of the sovereign, alleged in the pleading or declared to him by some who have authority from the sovereign power to declare them; and he need not take care beforehand what he shall judge, because it shall be given him what he shall say about the fact, by the witnesses, and what he shall say on a point of law, from those who in their pleadings shall set it forth, and by authority interpret it on the spot. The lords of Parliament in England were judges, and the most difficult cases have been heard and determined by them; yet few of them were much versed in the study of the laws, and fewer had made profession of them; and though they consulted with lawyers appointed to be present there for that purpose, they alone had the authority to give sentence. In the same way, in the ordinary trials of right, twelve men of the common people are the judges, and give sentence, not only of the fact but of the right, pronouncing simply for the complainant or for the defendant — that is, they are judges not only of the fact but also of the right; and in a question of crime, they not only determine whether it was done or not done, but also whether it was murder, homicide, felony, assault, and the like, which are determinations of law. But because they are not presumed to know the law of themselves, there is someone with authority to inform them of it in the particular case they are to judge. Yet if they do not judge according to what he tells them, they are not on that account subject to any penalty, unless it can be shown that they did it against their consciences, or had been corrupted by reward. The things that make a good judge, or a good interpreter of the laws, are: first, a right understanding of that principal law of nature called equity — which, depending not on the reading of other men's writings but on the goodness of one's own natural reason and meditation, is presumed to be most in those who have had the most leisure, and the most inclination, to meditate on it. Second, contempt of unnecessary riches and advancements in office. Third, the ability in judgement to divest himself of all fear, anger, hatred, love, and compassion. Fourth, and lastly, patience to hear; diligent attention in hearing; and memory to retain, digest, and apply what he has heard.

The difference and division of the laws has been made in various ways, according to the different methods of those who have written of them. For it is something that depends not on nature, but on the writer's scope, and is subordinate to every man's chosen method. In the Institutes of Justinian, we find seven sorts of civil laws.
1. The Edicts, Constitutions, and Letters of the Prince — that is, of the Emperor — because the whole power of the people resided in him. Like these are the proclamations of the kings of England.

2. The Decrees of the whole people of Rome (the Senate included), when they were put to the vote by the Senate. These were laws, at first, by virtue of the sovereign power residing in the people; and such of them as the emperors did not repeal remained laws by imperial authority. For every law that binds is understood to bind by the authority of whoever has the power to repeal it. Something like these laws are the Acts of Parliament in England.

3. The Decrees of the common people (excluding the Senate), when they were put to the vote by the tribune of the people. Such of these as the emperors did not repeal remained laws by imperial authority. Something like these were the Orders of the House of Commons in England.

4. Senatus consulta, the Orders of the Senate — because when the people of Rome grew so numerous that assembling them became inconvenient, the emperor thought it best that men consult the Senate in the people's place. These bear some resemblance to Acts of Council.
5. The Edicts of the Praetors, and in some cases of the Aediles — comparable to the Chief Justices in the courts of England.

6. Responsa Prudentum: the opinions and rulings of those lawyers to whom the emperor gave authority to interpret the law and to answer those who came to them in matters of law for advice. Judges, in delivering judgement, were bound by the emperor's constitutions to follow these rulings — they would be like the reports of decided cases, if other judges were bound by the law of England to follow them. For the judges of the common law of England are not, properly speaking, judges at all, but juris consulti — men of law whose advice the true judges, whether the Lords or twelve men of the country, are to seek on points of law.
7. Also, unwritten customs — which by their own nature imitate law — are, by the tacit consent of the emperor, true laws in themselves, provided they do not contradict the law of nature.

There is another division of laws, into natural and positive. Natural laws are those that have been laws from all eternity, and are called not only natural but also moral laws, consisting in the moral virtues — justice, equity, and all the habits of mind that promote peace and charity — of which I have already spoken in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

Positive laws are those that have not existed from eternity, but have been made laws by the will of those who have held sovereign power over others, and are either put in writing or otherwise made known to men as an expression of their legislator's will.

Again, of positive laws, some are human and some divine; and of human positive laws, some are distributive and some penal. Distributive laws are those that determine the rights of subjects, declaring to every man what it is by which he acquires and holds property in lands or goods, and a right or liberty of action — these speak to all subjects alike. Penal laws are those that declare what penalty shall be inflicted on those who break the law, and these speak to the ministers and officers appointed to carry out that execution. For although every man ought to be informed beforehand of the punishments set for his own transgression, the command itself is not addressed to the offender (who cannot be expected to punish himself faithfully), but to the public ministers charged with seeing the penalty carried out. These penal laws are for the most part written together with the distributive laws, and are sometimes called judgements — for all laws are general judgements, or sentences, of the legislator, just as every particular judgement is a law to the man whose case is judged.

Divine positive laws (for the natural laws, being eternal and universal, are all divine already) are those which, being commandments of God — not from all eternity, nor addressed to all men universally, but only to a certain people or to certain persons — are declared to be such by those whom God has authorised to declare them. But how can this authority of a man to declare what these positive laws of God are be known? God may command a man, by some supernatural means, to deliver laws to other men. But since it belongs to the very essence of law that the man who is to be obliged be assured of the authority of the one declaring it — and since we have no natural way of recognising that authority as coming from God — how can a man, without a revelation of his own, be assured of the revelation received by the one who declares it? And how can he be bound to obey it? As to the first question — how a man can be assured of another's revelation without a revelation particular to himself — the answer is plainly that he cannot. For although a man may be led to believe in such a revelation by the miracles he sees the other perform, or by the extraordinary holiness of his life, or by the extraordinary wisdom or extraordinary success of his actions (all of which are marks of God's special favour), none of these amount to assured evidence of a special revelation. Miracles are marvellous works, but what is marvellous to one man may not be so to another. Holiness can be feigned, and the visible good fortune of this world is, more often than not, the work of God through natural and ordinary causes. And so no man can know with certainty, by natural reason alone, that another has received a supernatural revelation of God's will — he can only believe it, more or less firmly, depending on how strong the signs of it appear to him.

But as to the second question — how he can be bound to obey it — that is not so hard. For if the law declared is not contrary to the law of nature (which is undoubtedly God's law), and he agrees to obey it, then he is bound by his own act — bound, I say, to obey it, but not bound to believe it. For men's beliefs and inward thoughts are not subject to command, but only to the working of God, whether ordinary or extraordinary. Faith in a supernatural law is not a fulfilling of that law, but merely an assenting to it — not a duty we render to God, but a gift God freely gives to whomever he pleases; just as unbelief is not the breaking of any of his laws, but a rejection of all of them except the natural ones. But what I am saying here will become still clearer through examples and testimonies on this point from Holy Scripture. The covenant God made with Abraham, in a supernatural manner, was this (Gen. 17:10): 'This is the covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your descendants after you.' Abraham's descendants had received no such revelation, and indeed did not yet exist; yet they were made party to the covenant, bound to obey whatever Abraham should declare to them as God's law — which they could only be bound to do by virtue of the obedience they already owed their parents, who (provided they were subject to no other earthly power, as was the case with Abraham) held sovereign power over their children and servants. Again, where God says to Abraham, 'In you shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, for I know that you will command your children and your household after you to keep the way of the Lord, and to observe righteousness and judgement,' it is plain that the obedience of his household, who had received no revelation of their own, rested on their prior obligation to obey their sovereign. At Mount Sinai, Moses alone went up to God; the people were forbidden to approach on pain of death; yet they were bound to obey everything Moses declared to them as God's law. On what ground, if not this submission of their own: 'Speak to us yourself, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die'? These two passages make it sufficiently clear that in a commonwealth, a subject who has no certain and assured revelation of his own concerning God's will is bound to accept as such the command of the commonwealth. For if men were free to take their own dreams and fancies — or the dreams and fancies of private individuals — as God's commandments, scarcely two men would agree about what God had commanded, and yet each would feel entitled, on that basis, to despise the commandments of the commonwealth. I conclude, therefore, that in everything not contrary to the moral law (that is, to the law of nature), all subjects are bound to obey as divine law whatever is declared to be such by the laws of the commonwealth. This is also plain to anyone's reason: for whatever is not against the law of nature may be made law in the name of those who hold sovereign power, and there is no reason why men should be any less obliged by it when it is put forward in the name of God. Besides, there is nowhere in the world where men are permitted to claim other commandments of God than those the commonwealth declares to be such. Christian states punish those who fall away from the Christian religion, and every other state punishes those who set up a religion it has forbidden. For in whatever the commonwealth has not regulated, it is equity — which is the law of nature, and therefore an eternal law of God — that every man should equally enjoy his liberty.

There is also another distinction of laws, into fundamental and not fundamental; but I have never seen, in any author, what a fundamental law actually means. Nevertheless, one may quite reasonably draw the distinction in this way.

A fundamental law, in any commonwealth, is one which, if removed, causes the commonwealth to fail and be utterly dissolved — like a building whose foundation has been destroyed. A fundamental law is therefore one by which subjects are bound to uphold whatever power has been given to the sovereign, whether a monarch or a sovereign assembly, without which the commonwealth cannot stand — such as the power of war and peace, of judicature, of the election of officers, and of doing whatever he judges necessary for the public good. A law is not fundamental if its repeal does not carry with it the dissolution of the commonwealth — such as the laws concerning disputes between one subject and another. So much, then, for the division of laws.

I find the words Lex Civilis and Jus Civile — that is, civil law and civil right — used interchangeably for the same thing, even by the most learned authors; though they should not be. For right is liberty — namely, that liberty which the civil law leaves us — but civil law is an obligation, and takes from us the liberty that the law of nature gave us. Nature gave every man a right to secure himself by his own strength, and to strike first against a neighbour he suspected; but civil law removes that liberty in every case where it is safe to wait instead for the protection of the law. So much, then, are Lex and Jus as different from one another as obligation is from liberty.

Likewise, laws and charters are interchangeably taken for the same thing. Yet charters are gifts from the sovereign, and are not laws but exemptions from law. The formula of a law is jubeo, injungo — 'I command,' 'I enjoin.' The formula of a charter is dedi, concessi — 'I have given,' 'I have granted.' But what is given or granted to a man is not forced upon him by a law. A law can be made to bind all the subjects of a commonwealth; a liberty, or charter, belongs only to one man, or to some one part of the people. For to say that all the people of a commonwealth have liberty in any case whatsoever is to say that, in that case, no law has been made — or else, having been made, has now been repealed.
